guideline.title: The diagnosis and management of primary mediastinal B-cell lymphoma: A British Society for Haematology guideline
guideline.citation: Osborne W, Bielby H, Cwynarski K, El-Sharkawi D, Petrides G, Illidge T, et al. Br J Haematol. 2026;209(4):1505–1517.
guideline.overview: PMBCL is an aggressive B-cell lymphoma of thymic B-cell origin. It mainly affects young adults, more often women, and its biology overlaps with classical Hodgkin lymphoma (9p24.1/PD-L1/PD-L2, JAK/STAT, NF-κB). This guideline updates the 2019 BSH good practice paper. It recommends dose-intensive chemoimmunotherapy (R-CHOP-14 or DA-R-EPOCH, not R-CHOP-21), PET-adapted radiotherapy (no RT after complete metabolic response, per IELSG37), a structured approach to Deauville 4 and 5 at end of treatment, thromboprophylaxis, and a relapse pathway built around CAR-T, with checkpoint inhibitors, bispecifics, loncastuximab, RT and transplant as further options.

recommendations.text: Offer participation in a clinical trial wherever possible.
Offer R-CHOP-14 × 6 or DA-R-EPOCH × 6.
R-CHOP-21 is not recommended.
Thromboprophylaxis is recommended in view of the high thrombotic risk.
Anti-microbial prophylaxis is recommended as per local practice.
Use conventional OSEM PET reconstruction techniques or specific research-accredited reconstructions for reporting the Deauville score on response assessment scans.
There are no current data to support a change of treatment as a result of interim PET response; therefore, the modality of interim imaging should be as per local clinical practice to assess response.
Do not offer radiotherapy for patients with DS 1–3 following chemoimmunotherapy.
Re-biopsy is recommended if feasible for all DS 4 and DS 5 patients at the EOT.

MDT discussion is essential to review the following: the heterogeneity of the DS 4 group—there is more concern regarding patients with SUV nearly 2× that of liver compared to just above liver; the site of disease and risk of radiotherapy; patient factors such as age and sex.
A personalised approach to balance the risk versus benefit of surveillance PET-CT or radiotherapy consolidation is required for patients with DS 4 at EOT.
Patients with DS 4 at EOT should be offered consultation with a clinical (radiation) oncologist to discuss radiotherapy versus surveillance imaging.
Discuss all patients with DS 5 at EOT at an MDT and perform a biopsy if possible. Offer systemic treatment as for relapsed disease for patients with DS 5.
Radiotherapy alone can be considered if there is limited single residual uptake on PET-CT without progression or if the patient is unfit for systemic chemotherapy.
Offer participation in a clinical trial wherever possible.
Offer CD19-directed targeted chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell (CAR-T) therapy (liso-cel) as second-line treatment if the patient has relapsed within 12 months.
Offer CD19-directed CAR T-cell therapy (axi-cel or liso-cel) as third or subsequent treatment line.
If available, consider the unlicensed combination of a PD1 inhibitor with brentuximab vedotin for patients with disease progression following CAR-T or autologous transplant.
Consider radiotherapy to localised sites of chemotherapy refractory disease.
Consider CD20-directed bispecific antibody with epcoritamab or glofitamab as a third or subsequent line of treatment line.
Consider loncastuximab as a third or subsequent line of treatment.
Consider allogeneic transplant for occasional patients who have failed multiple lines of treatment including CAR-T.
Consider discharge back to primary care for patients who are 24 months following end of treatment and who remain in remission.
Potential long-term complications should be outlined to patients and primary care health care professionals.
Do not perform surveillance imaging in asymptomatic patients.

topics.name: Presentation and thrombosis risk
topics.why: The typical patient (a young woman with an anterior mediastinal mass, SVCO or an effusion) and the 28% thrombosis rate are core facts.
keyPoints: PMBCL is a **mature, aggressive B-cell lymphoma of thymic B-cell origin**, with distinctive clinical, immunophenotypic and molecular features.
It arises in the **anterior mediastinum**, with variable extension to **lung, pleura and pericardium**. Regional nodes, often **supraclavicular**, may be involved.
**Bone marrow and extranodal involvement are uncommon at presentation** but more frequent **at relapse**.
Typical age is the **third or fourth decade**, with a **female predominance**.
Presentation: **pericardial or pleural effusions** (a **poor prognostic factor**), or **compressive symptoms including SVCO**.
**VTE is common, especially at presentation**: **28%** had thrombotic complications in a retrospective series of 156 adults and children.
**Prophylactic anticoagulation** is recommended if **platelets are >50 × 10⁹/L**, although evidence is limited. Use **therapeutic** anticoagulation for **proven thrombosis**.
There is **not enough evidence for routine therapeutic anticoagulation for venous compression alone**: decide **case by case**. Refer to the BSH cancer-associated thrombosis guideline.
numbers: platelet count above which prophylactic anticoagulation is recommended
pitfalls: Venous compression (e.g. SVCO) without proven thrombosis does not automatically need therapeutic anticoagulation. Decide case by case.
Effusions are a poor prognostic sign, not just a complication.
topics.hook: Young woman, front of the chest, squeezed SVC, sticky blood: 28% clot, so give prophylaxis if platelets are over 50.

selfTest.q: What thromboprophylaxis does the guideline recommend at PMBCL diagnosis?
selfTest.a: Prophylactic anticoagulation if platelets are >50 × 10⁹/L (thromboprophylaxis 1C), and therapeutic dosing for proven thrombosis.

selfTest.q: Which sites are uncommon at presentation but more frequent at relapse?
selfTest.a: Bone marrow and extranodal sites (the CNS is a site of rare late relapse).

topics.name: Diagnosis: biopsy, immunophenotype and molecular features
topics.why: Distinguishing PMBCL from cHL and grey zone lymphoma depends on the pattern of CD30, CD15, CD23 and PD-L1/L2 expression and on the 9p24.1 biology.
keyPoints: Differentials: **classical Hodgkin lymphoma, mediastinal grey zone lymphoma** and other B-cell lymphomas.

A **needle core** is often adequate (**14G, ideally ≥2 cores**), but tissue may run out before **FISH or molecular** testing. Some patients need a surgical biopsy. Review every case at an **MDT with a specialist haematopathologist**.
**Gene expression profiling** shows a signature that **overlaps with cHL** and differs from other aggressive lymphomas. Hallmarks are **NF-κB and JAK/STAT deregulation** and **immune escape**.
**Morphology:** diffuse sheets or clusters of medium to large cells with **abundant pale cytoplasm**, in a **fibrotic background**.

**Immunophenotype:** **CD45+** and B-cell antigens **CD19, CD20, CD22, CD79a**; transcription factors **BOB1, OCT2, PAX5**. **CD30** in most cases, but **weak and heterogeneous** (unlike cHL). Usually **IRF4+ and CD23+**. BCL6 and BCL2 variable. **CD10 uncommon (20–30%)**. **EBER negative**. Occasionally **CD15+**. **Thymic epithelial remnants** support the diagnosis. **PD-L1 and especially PD-L2** are typically expressed.

**Cytogenetics:** **CIITA rearrangements**, **REL amplification**, and **PD-L1 (CD274) / PD-L2 (PDCD1LG2)** copy number changes or rearrangements are generally specific. PD-L1 and PD-L2 sit on **9p24.1**, where **9p gain** is frequent. **JAK2**, upstream of PD-L1 on 9p24.1, further increases PD-ligand expression. **High PD-L1/L2 expression correlates with worse outcome.**
**BCL2, BCL6 and MYC rearrangements are rare or absent**, unlike in DLBCL.
The NHS England **National Genomic Test Directory** includes **REL copy number** and **PD-L1/PD-L2 rearrangement and copy number** by FISH, or a multitarget NGS panel.
numbers: locus of PD-L1, PD-L2 and JAK2
pitfalls: CD30 positivity does not make it Hodgkin: in PMBCL CD30 is weak and heterogeneous, and the cells keep a full B-cell programme (CD20, CD79a, OCT2, BOB1).
A MYC or BCL2 rearrangement makes PMBCL unlikely. Reconsider DLBCL or high-grade B-cell lymphoma.
topics.hook: PMBCL = B-cell body with a Hodgkin soul: CD20+, CD23+, weak CD30, EBER−, 9p24.1 gain driving PD-L1 and PD-L2.

selfTest.q: Which genetic changes are generally specific to PMBCL?
selfTest.a: CIITA rearrangements, REL amplification, and PD-L1/PD-L2 (9p24.1) copy gain or rearrangement.

selfTest.q: How does CD30 staining differ between PMBCL and cHL?
selfTest.a: In PMBCL, CD30 is usually weak and heterogeneous. In cHL it is strong on Hodgkin/Reed-Sternberg cells.

selfTest.q: Which gene is most frequently mutated in PMBCL on NGS?

topics.name: Staging, fertility and pregnancy
topics.why: Baseline PET before steroids underpins later Deauville decisions, and patients are young, so fertility planning matters.
keyPoints: **Baseline PET-CT in all patients before corticosteroids**, to assess the extent, volume and metabolic activity of disease.
**Do not withhold steroids in a clinical emergency.** CT staging is acceptable if waiting for PET would cause unacceptable delay in urgent cases.
Consider **contrast-enhanced CT** at baseline, especially if **vascular compromise or thrombosis** is suspected.
Marrow involvement is seldom seen, so **bone marrow biopsy is not mandated**. Consider it only if an alternative diagnosis is a concern. Blood tests are as in the BSH DLBCL guideline.
**Fertility:** ovarian dysfunction occurred during chemotherapy, but fertility was **preserved in most**. **Ovarian failure** occurred in some women **over 40**.
Offer **referral to a reproductive specialist before chemoimmunotherapy**. If urgency prevents this, still refer after treatment starts. Consider assessing gonadal function after treatment.
Males: offer **sperm banking** (testicular sperm extraction if no semen sample). Females: **embryo, oocyte or ovarian tissue cryopreservation**.

**Pregnancy:** manage with high-risk obstetricians and anaesthetists. Chemotherapy is riskiest in the **first trimester**. Small studies suggest regimens **without antimetabolites** can be given safely **after the second trimester**.
pitfalls: Steroids before baseline PET reduce its accuracy, but they should never be withheld in an emergency such as airway compromise or SVCO.
Bone marrow biopsy is not routine in PMBCL.
topics.hook: PET before pred, unless the patient is in danger.

selfTest.q: When is CT staging acceptable instead of baseline PET-CT?
selfTest.a: When waiting for PET would cause unacceptable delay in a clinically urgent case.

selfTest.q: What does the guideline say about chemotherapy in pregnancy?
selfTest.a: Manage jointly with high-risk obstetrics and anaesthesia. Regimens without antimetabolites may be safe after the second trimester. The first trimester carries the greatest risk.

topics.name: First-line chemoimmunotherapy
topics.why: Second-line therapy works poorly in PMBCL, so getting first-line right is the main determinant of cure. Dose-intensity matters.
keyPoints: First line is **dose- and time-intensive chemoimmunotherapy**: **R-CHOP-14, R-ACVBP or DA-R-EPOCH**.
**NCRI R-CHOP-14 vs 21** (PMBCL subgroup, n=50; 58% had ISRT): 5-year **PFS 79.8%**, **OS 83.8%**. Numerically better EFS with R-CHOP-14, but not significant (small numbers).
**LYSA pooled trials** (n=290): 4-year PFS **64% (R-CHOP-21) / 78% (R-CHOP-14) / 86% (R-ACVBP)**. Regimen was **independently prognostic**.
**Swedish registry:** benefit for R-CHOEP-14 and R-Hyper-CVAD over R-CHOP.
**Meta-analysis** (n=4068): **8% OS benefit** for dose-intensive regimens over CHOP ± R 21, **maintained only with rituximab-containing regimens**.

**DA-R-EPOCH** (Dunleavy, phase II, 51 + 16 patients): **EFS 93%, OS 97%, CR 96%**, with RT omitted unless progression. In the extended cohort (n=93), **25 had EOT DS4/5**: of **17 DS4, only 1 failed**; of **8 DS5, 4 failed**. So a single EOT PET has a **high false-positive rate**, and **serial PET with falling SUVmax** helps separate inflammation from residual disease.
**CALGB** phase III (DLBCL; only 6% PMBCL): **no efficacy difference** between R-CHOP and DA-R-EPOCH (including the PMBCL cohort, n=35), but **more toxicity** with DA-R-EPOCH.

**IELSG37** induction data: **R-CHOP-21** gave **more DS5 (23.8% vs 8.2%)** and **inferior EFS**. CMR rates were similar with R-CHOP-14 and DA-R-EPOCH, so **either is recommended** and **R-CHOP-21 should be avoided**. The trial was not powered to compare regimens.
**CNS prophylaxis is usually not needed** (low CNS-IPI). Indications are as in the BSH DLBCL guideline.
numbers: OS benefit of dose-intensive, rituximab-containing regimens (meta-analysis, n=4068)
DS5 rate with R-CHOP-21 vs other regimens (IELSG37)
pitfalls: R-CHOP-21, the DLBCL standard, is specifically not recommended in PMBCL (1B).
CALGB found no PMBCL benefit for DA-R-EPOCH, but the PMBCL numbers were small. The guideline still accepts DA-R-EPOCH or R-CHOP-14.

selfTest.q: Which first-line regimens are recommended in PMBCL, and which is not?
selfTest.a: R-CHOP-14 × 6 or DA-R-EPOCH × 6 (1B). R-CHOP-21 is not recommended (1B).

selfTest.q: In IELSG37, how did R-CHOP-21 perform compared with other inductions?
selfTest.a: More DS5 responses (23.8% vs 8.2% average) and inferior EFS.

selfTest.q: Is CNS prophylaxis routinely needed in PMBCL?
selfTest.a: No. Most patients have a low CNS-IPI. Indications are as for de novo DLBCL.

topics.name: Response assessment: interim and end-of-treatment PET
topics.why: Every radiotherapy decision depends on the end-of-treatment Deauville score, so how and when PET is done and reported matters.
keyPoints: Perform **interim imaging (CT or PET-CT)**. Interim PET is **prognostic** but must **not guide escalation or de-escalation**, because its positive predictive value is limited.
**EOT PET-CT at 6 weeks after cycle 6 day 1**, reported with **Deauville criteria**. If RT is given, assess with a **PET-CT 3 months after RT**.
**DS1–3 = complete metabolic response** (Lugano), with excellent prognosis. **DS4 = inflammation or lymphoma.** **DS5 = poor prognosis, usually lymphoma.**
DS5 definition: **IELSG37 used >2 × liver**. **Many UK centres use >3 × liver.**

**Advanced PET reconstruction** increases sensitivity and can **change Deauville scores**. Published PMBCL data used **conventional OSEM**, so report with OSEM-matched or research-accredited reconstructions until a harmonisation standard exists.
Report **lesion and liver SUVmax** so **ΔSUVmax** can be assessed. A significant fall in the DS4/5 group can be prognostic.
pitfalls: Do not change treatment because of interim PET (2B).
A newer high-sensitivity PET reconstruction can upgrade a score to DS4 or DS5 and lead to overtreatment. Use OSEM-matched reporting (1A).
topics.hook: Six weeks after C6D1, read with OSEM, report the SUVmax.

selfTest.q: When should the end-of-treatment PET be performed?
selfTest.a: 6 weeks after cycle 6 day 1, or 3 months after radiotherapy if RT is given.

selfTest.q: Why does the guideline insist on OSEM reconstruction?
selfTest.a: Published PMBCL Deauville data used OSEM. Advanced reconstructions are more sensitive and can change the score (1A).

topics.name: Radiotherapy after first line: DS1–3, DS4 and DS5
topics.why: IELSG37 changed practice: radiotherapy is no longer routine after complete metabolic response. DS4 is the grey zone that needs MDT judgement.
keyPoints: Second-line chemotherapy has limited efficacy, so first-line cure is key. But **routine consolidation RT for everyone would overtreat**, and the high **NPV of EOT PET** supports PET-guided RT.

**IELSG37:** of 545 patients in CMR by central review, **268 (49.2%)** were randomised to **observation (n=132) or RT (n=136)**. 30-month PFS was **96.2% vs 98.5%** (HR 1.47; 95% CI 0.34–6.28; absolute difference 0.68%). **5-year OS 99%** in both arms. So **omit RT after CMR**.
Not in CMR (50.8%): **DS4 PFS 95.8%**, similar to CMR (97.5%), but **86% of DS4 patients had RT**. **DS5**: 5-year **PFS 60.3%, OS 74.6%**.

**DS4 is heterogeneous**: SUV just above liver is less concerning than SUV nearly 2× liver. Options are **consolidation RT** or **repeat PET within 4–6 weeks**. A falling SUV may allow RT to be omitted. Melani: 1 of 17 DS4 patients progressed after DA-R-EPOCH. Royal Marsden: 2 of 9 DS4 patients progressed after R-CHOP-21.

**Personalise DS4 management** by age, sex, disease site, residual mass and lesion vs liver SUVmax, with the clinical oncologist, the patient and the MDT. **Biopsy if possible.** Most can have RT with low late toxicity, using **cardiac- and breast-sparing** techniques to residual PET-positive areas only.

If uptake is only minimally above liver and heart or breast dose cannot be avoided, **watch and wait** with interval PET or **DW-MRI** is reasonable. If there is no improvement, **biopsy and consider RT**. Do **not delay RT** if active disease is a concern. Consider the **psychological impact** of serial scans.

**DS5:** **re-biopsy** wherever possible. Most patients (progression or significant DS5 activity) get **systemic treatment as for relapse**. **RT alone** is an option for **limited single residual uptake without progression**, or when the patient is unfit for systemic therapy.
Technique: **deep inspiration breath hold (DIBH) photons**, or **protons** in selected cases.
numbers: 30-month PFS: observation vs RT after CMR (IELSG37)
PFS in DS4 vs CMR (86% of DS4 irradiated)
maximum interval for surveillance PET in DS4
DS4 SUV level of greater concern
pitfalls: Do not assume DS4 is lymphoma, or that it is only inflammation. Biopsy if feasible, then decide on RT or surveillance with the MDT.
DS5 usually needs relapse-type systemic therapy, not just radiotherapy.
topics.hook: 1–3: let it be. 4: think, biopsy, discuss. 5: biopsy and treat as relapse.

selfTest.q: What did IELSG37 show?
selfTest.a: In CMR (DS1–3) after chemoimmunotherapy, omitting RT gave no meaningful loss of PFS (96.2% vs 98.5% at 30 months) and the same 5-year OS (99%). So RT is not offered for DS1–3 (1A).

selfTest.q: List the factors the MDT should review for a DS4 patient.
selfTest.a: How far SUV is above liver (nearly 2× is more concerning), disease site and RT risk, and patient factors such as age and sex (1B). Biopsy if feasible, and offer a clinical oncology consultation (2A).

selfTest.q: When can RT alone be considered for DS5?
selfTest.a: Limited single residual uptake without progression, or if the patient is unfit for systemic chemotherapy (2B).

topics.name: Relapsed PMBCL: CAR-T and transplant
topics.why: Relapse is rare but early, and chemorefractoriness is common. CAR-T is now the main second-line option.
keyPoints: Relapse is **relatively rare**. Responses to second-line high-dose chemotherapy are **lower than in DLBCL**. Relapse is **almost always within 1 year**, and rare **late relapses often involve the CNS**. See the algorithms in **Figure 1** (first relapse) and **Figure 2** (second or later relapse).

**Liso-cel is licensed second line** and **NICE-approved for relapse within 12 months** of first-line treatment (TRANSFORM: 18 PMBCL patients, and 6 of 10 in the standard arm crossed over to liso-cel).
**Axi-cel is not approved second line** for PMBCL, because PMBCL was **excluded from ZUMA-7**.

**Third line: axi-cel or liso-cel** are both licensed. ZUMA-1: 8 of 101 had PMBCL, and 3 remained 'at risk' at 5 years. TRANSCEND: 15 PMBCL patients, **ORR 79%, CR 50%**, median DOR and PFS not reached.

**Real-world CAR-T (Table 1):** CART-SIE (70 PMBCL, better PFS and OS than LBCL, CR ~50%); axi-cel retrospective (33 patients, ORR 70%, CR 69%, 24-month PFS 64%); GLA/DRST (13 patients, ORR 85%, CR 54%); **DESCAR-T** (82 patients, CR 68%, 24-month PFS 71% with axi-cel); **CIBMTR** (135 patients, CR 67%, 24-month PFS 58.6%).

**Autologous transplant:** PMBCL is often **chemorefractory** second line, so many cannot reach it. **EBMT** (86 patients): 3-year PFS/OS **94%/100% if chemosensitive vs 39%/41% if chemoresistant**. MSKCC: 3-year PFS 60%, OS 65%. MD Anderson: 5-year PFS 58% in responders.

**Allogeneic transplant** can give durable remissions. In a Belgian/French series (33 patients), PFS was 47% and OS 48%, and disease status at transplant was the key predictor. In a US series (28 patients), 5-year PFS was 34% and OS 45%, rising to 50% and 58% if chemosensitive.

numbers: EBMT 3-year PFS/OS after ASCT: chemosensitive vs chemoresistant
pitfalls: Axi-cel is not a second-line option in PMBCL. Liso-cel is (ZUMA-7 excluded PMBCL).
A late relapse in PMBCL should prompt a search for CNS disease.
topics.hook: Early relapse (<12 months): liso-cel. Later lines: axi-cel or liso-cel. ZUMA-7 left PMBCL out.

selfTest.q: Which CAR-T is licensed second line for PMBCL, and why not the other?
selfTest.a: Liso-cel, for relapse within 12 months (1C). Axi-cel is not approved second line because PMBCL was excluded from ZUMA-7.

selfTest.q: How does chemosensitivity affect ASCT outcome in PMBCL (EBMT)?
selfTest.a: 3-year PFS/OS was 94%/100% if chemosensitive vs 39%/41% if chemoresistant.

topics.name: Relapse: checkpoint inhibitors, bispecifics, ADCs and radiotherapy
topics.why: The PD-L1/L2 biology makes checkpoint inhibitors uniquely useful in PMBCL. Know which other agents work and which do not.
keyPoints: **Radiotherapy in relapsed or refractory disease** is increasingly used. A meta-analysis of 12 studies gave 2-year **PFS 95% and OS 97%**. Follow **ILROG** principles. **Give RT after transplant**, not before, because of **pneumonitis risk**. Use butterfly IMRT/VMAT, protons and **DIBH** to spare lung, heart and breast.
**Loncastuximab** (anti-CD19 ADC) is licensed and commissioned **third line onwards** (LOTIS-2, which **excluded bulky disease**). Only 1 of 7 PMBCL patients had a PR, with a PFS of 1.35 months.

**Bispecifics (CD3 × CD20): glofitamab and epcoritamab** are licensed **third line+**. Glofitamab: CR 39% overall and **50% in the PMBCL subgroup** (6 patients). Glofitamab plus polatuzumab: 2 patients in CMR at 5 months.
**Brentuximab alone works poorly** despite CD30 expression: **2 of 15 responded, with no CRs**.

**Pembrolizumab:** KEYNOTE-013 ORR **48%**, CR 33% (n=21). KEYNOTE-170 ORR **45%**, CR 13% (n=53), rising to **21%** with more than 4 years' follow-up. **No CR patient relapsed.** Median PFS was 4.3 months.

**Nivolumab + brentuximab (CheckMate 436, n=30):** **ORR 73%, CR 40%**, median PFS **26 months**. 12 proceeded to transplant, and 4 stayed in long-term remission without consolidation. Real-world data (n=14) match these results.
Case reports describe **nivolumab with RT** or with **high-dose chemotherapy**.
numbers: 2-year PFS / OS with RT in R/R PMBCL (meta-analysis)
glofitamab CR in the PMBCL subgroup
pitfalls: CD30 is expressed in PMBCL, but single-agent brentuximab is ineffective. Its activity comes when it is combined with a PD-1 inhibitor.
Irradiating before high-dose therapy and ASCT increases pneumonitis risk. Irradiate after transplant.
topics.hook: 9p24.1 explains why PD-1 blockade works. Brentuximab needs a PD-1 partner.

selfTest.q: What is the guideline's position on PD-1 inhibitor plus brentuximab?
selfTest.a: If available, consider the unlicensed combination for progression after CAR-T or autologous transplant (2C). CheckMate 436 showed ORR 73% and CR 40%.

selfTest.q: When should RT be given relative to transplant in relapsed PMBCL, and why?
selfTest.a: After transplant, because RT before high-dose therapy increases the risk of pneumonitis.

topics.name: Follow-up and survivorship
topics.why: Most relapses happen within 12 months, so follow-up can be short and should not include routine scans.
keyPoints: **Most relapses occur within 12 months**, so patients still in remission at **24 months** may be **discharged to primary care**.
**Re-scan only for new symptoms or signs** suggesting relapse. **No surveillance imaging** in asymptomatic patients.
Tell patients and GPs about **long-term complications**, such as **cardiac toxicity and second malignancies**, so they are referred promptly if symptoms arise.
pitfalls: Routine surveillance PET or CT in asymptomatic patients is not recommended (1B).
topics.hook: Two years clear: back to the GP, and no routine scans.

selfTest.q: When can PMBCL patients be discharged to primary care?
selfTest.a: Once they are 24 months after end of treatment and still in remission (2C).

selfTest.q: Which long-term complications should patients and GPs be told about?
selfTest.a: Cardiac toxicity and second malignancies, among others.
